#6547. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6546. Caramelized Cabbage Pasta

This pasta is the easiest way to cram an entire head of cabbage into one comforting dinner. The secret? Cooking it in butter over a long, relaxed period of time until it softens into a decadent, caramelized tangle. Paired with spaghetti, heavy cream, and some Dijon mustard and lemon zest to brighten everything up, this dish is a celebration of how versatile cabbage can be. Feel free to top your bowl with lots of fresh dill, or leave it unadorned with nothing more than an extra sprinkle of cheese.

Cook 12 oz. spaghetti in a large pot of boiling generously salted water, stirring occasionally, until very al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid. Set aside.

Melt 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pot over high heat. Add 1 large head of green cabbage (about 3 lb.), cored, thinly sliced, and 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring often, until cabbage is very tender and browned in spots, 18–25 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup), 1½ cups heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and reserved pasta to cabbage and toss to coat. If sauce is too thick, add pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time, tossing constantly, until glossy. Taste pasta and season with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with finely chopped dill if desired.

#6544. Is This Department Stores’ Big Comeback Christmas?

Gone are the days of the branded luxury Christmas window.

In an era where department stores need to work harder than ever to get a holiday shopper into their store — rather than them shopping online, directly with a brand, or at the department store up the road — many retailers are branching out beyond the monobrand Christmas window strategy that’s dominated recent holiday seasons.

Last week, stores from Bergdorf Goodman to Bloomingdale’s made a splash with their holiday window unveilings. Saks followed suit on Monday, November 23. The weather was unseasonably warm, with attendees clad in light jackets, rather than the usual fur and puffers for this time of year. Bergdorf made up for the tepid temps with fake snow. Bloomingdale’s had Sienna Spiro sing a rendition of “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas”.

By going the multibrand route, stores can put themselves at the center of their holiday storytelling, and appeal to a wider range of consumers by displaying merchandise across a host of different price points. Utilizing existing merchandise is also a lower lift than the logistical and financial burden of staging a full brand takeover. “I’m anticipating highly creative windows with a variety of merchandise. The general sentiment as of the last several months is that the customer shops high and low, where two years ago it was all about the big labels,” says luxury consultant Robert Burke. “So I think you’re going to see a variety of merchandise displayed in creative ways.”

It’s panning out. Nordstrom is partnering with David Bowie’s estate to celebrate what would be the star’s 80th birthday — and is Nordstrom’s 125th anniversary. Included in Bowie80 are collaborations with designers including Paul Smith, Marc Jacobs and Undercover’s Jun Takahashi. Bergdorf Goodman’s windows are a vignette inspired by a New York winter, celebrating 125 years with an array of capsules from brands including Michael Kors, Brunello Cucinelli and Valentino. Saks’s windows offer up a tour of the festive period in the city. Over in London, Liberty is leaning into storytelling around holiday rituals and routines, and Selfridges is, like its peers, celebrating wintertime in the city (New York City, that is).

Bergdorf invited a host of designers to participate in its holiday window unveiling.

Not all of the players are going wide, though. Bloomingdale’s Friday window unveiling was in partnership with Ralph Lauren. Partnering with Ralph was a no-brainer, says Kevin Harter, VP of integrated marketing. “Ralph Lauren is synonymous with the traditions, nostalgia and timelessness that makes the holidays so special,” she says. The evening included a festive Ralph cocktail in the store — with teddy bear sweaters aplenty — and David Lauren was onstage to celebrate the unveiling alongside Bloomingdale’s CEO Olivier Bron. Inside, though, there are an array of brand activations — over 50 — from Barbour’s Tea & Sympathy pop-up to Ugg’s takeover of the Bloomingdale’s restaurant — and famed froyo destination — Forty Carrots. (There’s an Ugg-exclusive flavor, of course.) Ralph Lauren is the anchor, Harter says.

Overall, this multibrand, amped-up storytelling logic extends to the in-store experience itself. Department stores this season have built out their holiday strategies around curation, with the view of inspiring their customers with the creative while making their lives as easy as possible. “One of the biggest opportunities for retail at Christmas is getting the balance between inspiration and ease right,” says Lydia King, managing director of retail at Liberty.

This is especially important this year, after department stores weathered quieter holiday seasons amid the upheaval of recent years. 2026 started with a bang, as Saks Global declared bankruptcy in January and, since summer, has been pushing its comeback as Exemplar Luxury Group. Bloomingdale’s, too, has spent 2026 pushing upmarket, making the most of a moment in which many of its contemporaries are struggling to meet the moment. This festive period, the stakes are high, capping off a year in which US department stores sought to regain lost magic.

Here’s how department stores are meeting the moment for this all-important holiday season.

This season, retailers are placing emphasis on their curation for the holiday period. The single-brand focus made sense a few years back when luxury was at its peak, Burke says. But now, he argues, department stores are looking to be more democratic in price point and product. “Compared to a few years ago, I’m seeing a lot of interest in smaller brands and independent brands,” he says. “The luxury customer today, even at the highest level, their mindset is very open to not having to only have major luxury branded merchandise.”

Department stores are curating more than just product, though. Across the board — and in keeping with Gen Z’s desire for shopping experiences that offer meaning and excitement inaccessible via social media — they’re placing emphasis on the unique experiences offered in-store throughout the holidays.

Nordstrom’s holiday facade is an embrace of Bowie.

In doing so, they’re putting themselves at the center of the narrative. Bergdorf Goodman is doing this literally, placing the store in the middle of its New York-themed holiday campaign and window display which, this year, literally leads shoppers inside. “After the sidewalk introduces you to the narrative, it continues through the main doors into a Zhivago-esque wintry snow-laden forest hung with rock crystal chandeliers and a flock of white geese overhead,” says Linda Fargo, SVP of Bergdorf’s fashion office and store presentation.

“This year we’ve put much more emphasis on the whole experience of Christmas at Liberty, beyond the product offering,” says Liberty’s King. The store’s campaign, The Liberty Christmas Chronicles, follows the rituals of the season — preparing, dressing, traveling, gathering, unwinding and eventually resting — with gifting running throughout, of course. “We know customers increasingly value curation, personalization and expertise,” she says.

This comes in via mini in-store experiences, from wreath-making with Diptyque (Liberty’s hero partner in its Atrium section) to build-your-own hampers in the Liberty Food Hall. Other activations include personalized bows with Moët & Chandon, lipstick engraving with Lisa Eldridge and makeup bag embroidery with Westman Atelier.

Selfridges is taking a similar multibrand approach with tailored, ‘only available here’ experiences. With Canada Goose on Duke Street, for instance, the retailer has constructed an Arctic-inspired research outpost with hot chocolates and personalized luggage tags, and the ultra-buzzy Vice City GTA VI pop-up kicked off the retailer’s holiday activities.

“These partnerships help create a Christmas that feels distinctive to Selfridges,” says marketing and experiences director Rebecca Warburton. “We know that people are looking for experiences, opportunities to connect with others and to create memorable moments,” she says, noting that Selfridges looked to offer more reasons for customers to spend time at the store this season.

Saks is leaning into these in-person experiences more than ever. For the first time, L’Avenue at Saks will host breakfast with Santa throughout the season and will transform into Le Chalet, with festive menu programming, on holiday season weekends.

Sienna Spiro performed at the Bloomingdale’s x Ralph Lauren window unveiling.

This curation extends to stores’ gifting options. Beyond offering a smart selection of brands, stores are also thinking more deeply about their non-fashion gifting options, so that customers will shop with them not just for shoes, but for stocking stuffers, too.

Bergdorf Goodman does this well, Burke says, noting the store’s “tremendous” holiday season in 2025. “Bergdorf’s home floor is a very good example of it being a tourist destination with fun Christmas merchandise, because they sell all of these Christmas ornaments, candies and candles. It takes over the entire seventh floor,” he says. In celebration of its 125th anniversary, Bergdorf is upping the ante this year with an Assouline legacy book, Very Bergdorf, ‘Very Bergdorf’ specialty ornaments, plus a snow globe featuring the Bergdorf Goodman facade. “Every part of the store has something uniquely made for us, and it all adds up to a very Bergdorf holiday,” Fargo says.

This year, Nordstrom is partnering with toy companies including FAO Schwarz and Jellycats. “You think about a retailer being relevant and having all the things customers want to buy — particularly at the holidays — partnerships like that help, in addition to carrying the best brands in the world,” says Deniz Anders, EVP, chief marketing officer. “Being able to check off their list for everyone across the family, that’s something that we’re really focused on.” Nordstrom has also invested more in consumables this year, and has a partnership with fashion-favorite Flamingo Estate.

This season, department stores are thinking more than ever about ease. Saving customers time and effort, execs believe, is the way to capture their hearts — and their spend.

Nordstrom has expanded its gift shops in common areas throughout the store. “It’s really not something that we used to do, but we want customers to know this is a place that you can buy gifts at broad price points,” Anders says. The retailer tested the cross-store setup last year and has expanded the size of the shops this season. “We want to make it easy and fun for customers to buy gifts.”

Liberty’s largest holiday season development is the introduction of its Gifting Curator service, King says. “For the first time, customers can book one-to-one appointments with Liberty experts who can guide them across the whole store, rather than within a single category or brand,” she says. “The idea is to make discovering the right present feel as special as giving it.” To round out the experience, Liberty has introduced a gift-wrapping experience with wrapper Roxy Wraps.

Stores have also been planting seeds to get their customers in the shopping mindset. Though all of the big, splashy window displays were unveiled at their usual time, just before Thanksgiving, the communications around the holiday season started far earlier. Nordstrom sent out its holiday catalog a week earlier than usual, Anders says. It’s the retailer’s biggest catalog ever. “We’ve been bringing in gifts a lot earlier,” she says. “Holiday is a marathon and you’ve got to have the gifts early and be ready to serve customers and bring a little joy and fun.”

#6543. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6541. Red-Wine-Braised Short Ribs

These red-wine-braised short ribs have fans. “This has been my go-to recipe for short ribs for as long as I can remember,” says one commenter. “It never fails.” It’s the kind of special-occasion dish you make once and return to forever.

Flavor builds in layers: The bone-in beef is browned, then the onions, carrots, and celery cook in its drippings. A full bottle of dry red wine reduces by half before the broth goes in; a whole head of garlic and plenty of fresh herbs round out the braise. After that, a few hours in the oven turn the meat fall-off-the-bone tender.

Even better: You can make the ribs a day ahead, leaving little to do before dinner but reheat them. Serve over mashed potatoes, soft polenta, or wide egg noodles to soak up every drop of the rich sauce.

Look for meaty, bone-in English-cut short ribs, with a single rib bone beneath each piece of meat. Ask your butcher to cut them crosswise into 2" lengths—you’re not expected to saw through the bones at home. Avoid the thin strips sold for grilling.

What’s the best wine for braised short ribs?

Choose a dry red wine you’d enjoy drinking. Cabernet Sauvignon is the recipe’s first choice, but Merlot or a Rhône-style red also fits the bill. There’s no need to splurge; save your special bottle for the table.

For the smooth sauce intended here, yes. The vegetables flavor the braising liquid, and straining removes them along with the herb stems, bay leaves, and garlic skins.

For a more rustic approach, pluck out the herbs and garlic skins (leave the cloves behind) and use an immersion blender to purée the cooked vegetables into the sauce.

Start checking after 2 hours in the oven. A fork should slide into the meat easily, and a gentle twist should pull it apart. If the meat still resists, keep braising. The listed cooking time is a guide, not a hard stop.

Can I make these short ribs ahead, and how should I reheat them?

Yes. Finish cooking the ribs and strain the sauce, then refrigerate the ribs with their sauce in shallow containers within 2 hours of cooking. The next day, lift off the hardened fat. Transfer the ribs and sauce to an ovenproof pot or baking dish, cover, and reheat in a 350° oven until hot throughout—the meat should reach 165° in the center.

Save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app

Try this recipe with this expert pick from the Bon Appétit Wine Shop.

Staub Enameled Cast Iron Round Dutch Oven 7-Qt.

Preheat oven to 350°. Season 5 lb. bone-in beef short ribs, cut crosswise into 2" pieces by your butcher, with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Working in 2 batches, cook short ribs, turning occasionally, until browned on all sides, about 8 minutes per batch. Transfer to a plate. Pour off all but 3 Tbsp. drippings from pot.

Cook 3 medium onions, chopped, 3 medium carrots, peeled, chopped, and 2 celery stalks, chopped, in same pot over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onions are browned, about 5 minutes. Add 3 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and 1 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until combined and deep red, 2–3 minutes.

Stir in one 750-ml bottle dry red wine (preferably Cabernet Sauvignon), then add short ribs along with any juices that have accumulated on the plate. Bring to a boil; reduce heat to medium and simmer until wine is reduced by half, about 25 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, halved crosswise, 10 sprigs parsley, 8 sprigs thyme, 4 sprigs oregano, 2 sprigs rosemary, and 2 fresh or dried bay leaves; stir in 4 cups low-sodium beef broth. Bring to a boil, cover, and transfer pot to oven. Braise until short ribs are tender, 2–2½ hours.

Uncover pot and transfer short ribs to a platter. Strain sauce through a fine-mesh sieve into a heatproof measuring glass; spoon fat from surface and discard. Season sauce with salt and pepper. Arrange ribs in shallow bowls, over mashed potatoes if desired, and spoon sauce over.

#6540. ‘Political malpractice’: Calls grow to delay Senate GOP leadership elections

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

“After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said on Monday evening.

Asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”

Though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

“Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I said, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”

Johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

Also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”

Kennedy said Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he said, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”

But Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, said she has seen such requests launched in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

And several Senate GOP aides said that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the plans and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

That includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”

Republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott said. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

An online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”

Banks similarly said Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”

One senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” said Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”

#6539. Setting Up Shop in Istanbul

In Istanbul, hosts encourage guests to stay as long as they like — even in luxury department stores. “We want our client to spend time here, to sit here, to play backgammon, to chat, to have a drink,” says Sebla Refiğ Devidas, chief merchandising officer at Communité, a new concept-department store hybrid, first opened in April of this year, with two outposts on the European side of the city. “We wanted to give a homey, warm feeling,” she adds, guiding me through the retailer’s second location, opened in May. Unlike many of Istanbul’s retail spaces, the store features windows throughout, letting natural sunlight fill the curving, geometric shop-in-shops, clean furnishings, and marble plinths. We pass rails of brands including Martine Rose, Simone Rocha and Auralee, as well as a warmly lit Mayfair-style restaurant, a glass-paneled red-light therapy salon and box vitrines of jewellery by Turkish jewellery designer Sevan Bıçakçı.

The store is located in Galataport, a cultural and shopping district adjacent to the Bosphorus, the strait separating Türkiye’s European and Asian sides. Galataport is also home to a number of luxury players. Beymen — Türkiye’s answer to Bergdorf Goodman — has an outpost. There’s also a Vakkorama, the luxury retailer Vakko’s accessible, contemporary store. And Turkish design-focused luxury chain Gizia Gate. Together, these four names (Communité, Beymen, Vakko and Gizia Gate) define the Turkish fashion landscape, taking the lion’s share of a relatively small fashion retail market.

Beyond luxury retail, Istanbul and Türkiye are widely renowned for their role in the textile and leather industries, home to a large portion of the major clothing manufacturers used by Western brands, including Isko Denim, Kipaş and Bilsar. Value-seeking shoppers also enjoy the region’s stores specializing in factory seconds — lightly defective branded apparel sold at a discount — and counterfeit luxury goods available in the historic Grand Bazaar, where sellers are naturally averse to photography.

Sebla Refiğ Devidas (left) works as the chief merchandizing officer at Communité.

Istanbul has a population of more than 15 million people, while Türkiye has over 86 million. According to data from Euromonitor, Türkiye’s market for luxury goods delivered steady growth in 2025, recovering from continued macroeconomic pressures. High-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) remained a core driver for growth, while inflation — exacerbated by the Middle East crisis — dragged on discretionary spending for middle-income groups. The report also cited Gucci, Hermès, Prada and Louis Vuitton as some of the leading international brands in the personal luxury goods category. In 2026, Euromonitor forecasts luxury sales to reach almost $28 billion in 2026, over double the revenue in 2021.

“Istanbul sits at the heart of this opportunity, supported by growing domestic wealth alongside its strength as an international shopping, hospitality and cultural destination,” says Fflur Roberts, Euromonitor International’s head of luxury. Tourism is becoming particularly important, she adds, noting that international visitors now account for 29% of personal luxury goods spending in Türkiye, up from 20% in 2019. “Wealthy Russian travelers have contributed to this shift, as geopolitical developments redirect travel and luxury spending toward markets including Türkiye and the UAE.”

Outside Communité’s new location in Galataport.

Currently, Roberts reports, online channels account for 21% of personal luxury sales in Türkiye — which is more than double the share in 2015. “Yet physical retail remains important, giving Istanbul an opportunity to combine global luxury brands with Turkish fashion, craftsmanship, hospitality, gastronomy and culture as consumers increasingly blend shopping with travel and experiences,” Roberts affirms.

Within this relatively small retail pond, luxury retail competition is fierce.

And competition is heating up. Communité will open two more stores on the European side and one on the Asian side in 2027, complementing a strong online presence. The retailer is owned by Boyner, which originally founded Beymen in 1970. Beymen has now changed ownership: since 2015, the Qatari fund Mayhoola has been investing in the retailer, eventually taking control in 2019.

Inside Communité, clients can inquire about buying the furniture.

Devidas was a merchandising lead at Beymen, but in August 2024, following a five-year non-compete clause, she and many of her former colleagues from Boyner jumped ship to the newly founded Communité. “We didn't want to repeat what we had done,” she says. “But we wanted to create something new from scratch.” During the research stage, the team traveled the globe, informing their objectives for clienteling, product assortments and dwell time. Hospitality will prove integral to its value proposition, she says.

Insiders respect it, too. Cemre Bosnalı Zeydanlı, Vogue Türkiye’s strategy editor, pinpoints the retailer as exemplary of Türkiye’s retail development: “With its locations at İstinye Park and Galataport, the concept goes beyond traditional multi-brand retail by bringing together fashion, beauty, design, culture and lifestyle.”

On my visit to Communité, Devidas tells me that much of the furniture in the store is available to buy. There are Turkish brands — Lug Von Siga, for example — alongside mega international brands, including Japanese streetwear giant A Bathing Ape (Bape), which Devidas says is a Communité exclusive in Türkiye.

Taking a more traditionally luxe approach, Beymen Group is ramping up its retail presence across the country. The retail giant owns 290 stores in various formats across Türkiye and Egypt (a small operation): 25 multi-brand, 60 franchise stores with leading designer brands, and three of its own brands. The expansion is in progress.

During my stay in the city, Beymen underscores its luxury ambitions with a ritzy event program, built around a new exhibition, Timeless Treasures — an homage to traditional Anatolian envelope bags through the lens of contemporary Western and local designers — at its flagship location in the wealthy shopping and hospitality district of Tersane. The exhibition coincides with the OMA-designed store’s first anniversary and intends to bridge a gap between the Turkish and global fashion landscape.

Toasting the occasion, Beymen invited industry authorities and fashion designers Giuseppe Zanotti, Giuseppe Santoni and Antonin Tron to a black-tie gala. During the evening, brand execs rubbed shoulders with Beymen group’s senior leadership team as group CEO Elif Çapçı outlined her vision for Beymen and the future of Türkiye’s fashion landscape. Diana Ross performed afterwards.

High-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) typically lead consumer spending for Beymen, and the company — thanks to Mayhoola’s investment — is courting this, enhancing its store experiences and private-shopping service. Beymen has no plans to expand globally and will focus almost entirely on Türkiye.

Beymen’s Tersane location was designed with the Office for Metropolitan Architecture (OMA).

The reason for Beymen’s focus on the home market? It needs to feel rooted in the location. “The department store is more like a house that you bring people to,” says Rachid Mohamed Rachid, Mayhoola CEO and chairman for Valentino and Balmain. “People have to be comfortable with the culture, with the DNA, with the approach.” This fiscal year, the group is close to making €1.5 billion, growing at 15% in the first nine months.

While Communité’s footprint doesn’t quite compete with Beymen, Vakko’s — opened first as a small hat shop in 1934 — does. As of March 31, the company has 150 stores and remains a household name in Türkiye. The company offers a variety of categories, own-brand goods and store formats including Vakkorama, Vakko Couture (a fashion-forward boutique) and the original Vakko luxury stores.

Tarik, 28, works in Vakkorama’s Galataport location. He explains that customers engage with the retailer for its fashion-forward choice of brands evidenced in the V2K Designers range — Marni, Thom Browne, JW Anderson, for example — as well as unique pieces from brands, such as Adidas, that can’t be found elsewhere in the country.

“I think multi-brand stores such as V2K Designers play an important role in Istanbul’s fashion ecosystem,” says Zeydanlı. ”Being able to explore collections from different designers in one place brings a more curated perspective to shopping.”

Vakko — which own sub-brands V2K, Vakkorama, and Vakko Couture — is one of the big four in the Turkish retail market.

For local Turkish designers, landing one of the big four wholesalers can be hard, especially if you’re an emerging voice. When Gul Agis, the designer behind established Turkish brand Lug Von Siga, started out 17 years ago after studying in Italy, she actually focused on reaching stores across mainland Europe, taking part in fashion weeks and trade shows in Berlin, Paris and Milan. “It was quite challenging for me because where Milan was quite professional in prêt-à-porter, it was almost the beginning here [in Istanbul],” she remembers. “Most of the fashion houses or designers used to do more haute couture or made-to-measure pieces.”

At the time, she says that the major Turkish retailers tended to focus on foreign brands. Fast forward to now, and a lot has changed. Lug Von Siga has since been stocked by Beymen and Gizia Gate, although those partnerships have now ended. Today, she works with Vakko and Communité, plus a myriad of European stockists including Harvey Nichols, Farfetch and Harrods.

Vakkorama’s Galataport location faces a waterway used by cruise ships.

Istanbul’s retail landscape is big on malls, comprising key new-build districts such as Tersane, Galataport and Zorlu Center. Shoppers take their time while purchasing, sipping coffee or Turkish tea, and store advisors provide discretion and advice where necessary for private clients. The shopping experience is slower and more relaxed, compared to fashion hubs like London and New York.

Consumers in Istanbul rely on malls such as Zorlu Center on the European side.

Beyond these purpose-built complexes, Istanbul is also home to an even more easygoing, hilly, open shopping district, Nişantaşı, on the European side of the city. Here, Prada, Chanel, Beymen, Vakko, and other major players have stores, as well as a substantial number of concept stores. Turkish fashion photographer Fırat Koçak, who joins me on the journey, describes Nişantaşı as a trendier district, with many editors, stylists and photographers living here. National treasure designer Ozgur Masur’s showroom is here, as well as Agis’s.

Nişantaşı’s Shopi Go is a perennial hangout for cool kids. Opened in 2012 in a former Chinese food joint, complete with exposed-brick walls, the cozy two-story store is arranged with coffee-table books, knick-knacks, and niche fashion apparel. Y-3’s cleat football sneakers, Wales Bonner x Umbro designs, and pieces from underground Turkish label Doomster fill the space. It’s charmingly dingy, and the product assortment is esoteric, clearly aimed at a more niche Turkish consumer.

Shopi Go is a Chinese-food-spot-turned concept store.

Shopi Go is aimed at the more directional Turkish consumer, offering Wales Bonner x Umbro through to local brand Doomster.

A few blocks away, two smiling buyers — Emir Akdogan and Dylon Kader — sit outside the streetwear store Wunder’s largest location. They’ve agreed to show me around. Inside, the architecture is restrained, cold and contemporary — a far cry from the more luxe DTC stores peppered elsewhere in the area. Wunder’s first store opened in 2015 in Kadikoy, a district on the Asian side, and quickly capitalized on the sneaker boom. In 2021, Wunder opened the Nişantaşı store. Today, it continues to push anticipated sneakers from Nike (including Jordan) and Salomon, as well as streetwear from brands including Stüssy, Carhartt and Stockholm Surfboard Club.

“I assume we are the only super-contemporary store, rather than a department store [in Istanbul], which makes us slightly different,” says Akdogan. “Still, sneakers are a huge part of the business,” says Kader. “We were one of the stores that had camps — first come, first served. People put tents in the streets. It was so new to the Turkish community, and the Turkish market, so it was not done before.”

In Istanbul, stray cats are treated with reverence and free neutering. They’re not typically allowed in stores, though.

Akdogan and Kader describe the Turkish market as a little slower to catch on to hot European market trends. The pair tells me that they had to convince the Salomon global team to come to Türkiye. When Salomon agreed, two to three years ago, Wunder began selling the brand. “The first three or four seasons, it didn’t sell at all — even with discounts,” remembers Kader. “Then last season, something happened. People started to ask for Salomons, and we started to bump up our orders.”

The buyers want to set trends and be global, but contend that does involve some business sacrifice as the national market catches up with global trends. That said, the most loyal consumer for Wunder is an educated shopper, the pair confirm.

Emir Akdogan and Dylon Kader are buyers at Wunder, one of the original streetwear stores in the city.

“Türkiye is a dynamic market for fashion and luxury, but one shaped by its own economic and cultural nuances,” says Zeydanlı. “One of the most interesting aspects of the Turkish market, in my opinion, is the consumer’s interest in both global fashion houses and local designers.” Zeydanlı encourages brands looking to enter the Turkish market to understand local consumer expectations, developing the right pricing strategy to handle growing price sensitivity among consumers.

Beymen’s chief merchandising officer, Ahmet Öcal, explains that the company’s buying strategy is rooted in a deep understanding of their clients’ lifestyles. “We serve a diverse and increasingly sophisticated customer base through Beymen’s extensive brand curation and personalized service approach, ranging from established luxury clients who value heritage, craftsmanship and timeless elegance, to younger, fashion-forward consumers who are looking for newness, individuality and self-expression,” he explains, noting that the core consumer base is local, while 15% are international tourists.

“Occasion wear, elevated casualwear, luxury handbags, jewelry, cosmetics, and beauty are particularly relevant categories for our market,” says Öcal. “Resort wear is another important area, reflecting the lifestyle of our customers and their connection to destinations like Bodrum.”

“When it comes to clienteling, I believe the emphasis should be on genuinely understanding the customer: their personal style, preferences and shopping habits,” says Zeydanlı. “Curated product selections, early access to new collections, private shopping appointments, and invitations to exclusive brand experiences all play an important role.” This chimes with the kind of customer engagement strategies Beymen employs, maintaining close and enduring relations with top spenders, many of whom have shopped there for years.

Across the board, luxury players cite millennials as a strong consumer in the Turkish retail landscape, particularly those within the 30 to 40 bracket. Beymen’s target consumer is roughly 35-plus. That said, players should ensure they speak to younger generations. For Zeydanlı, Gen Z might not have the strongest purchasing power yet, but they remain a key consumer group shaping the future of luxury. “Gen X, meanwhile, remains an important segment, particularly among high-net-worth consumers, thanks to more established luxury shopping habits and stronger brand loyalty,” she says.

The city of Istanbul is relatively young in the global luxury retail market, despite its strong manufacturing heritage. “However, on the design side, we are lacking certain components that would make our designers global names and successful on a global scale,” says Mayhoola’s Rachid. “The visibility is not there.”

Setting up shop here as a local independent designer remains risky, although it’s improving. Across the board, international household names rule the market.

However, as the market grows, tastes could shift. While Beymen might choose to focus its efforts on the local demand, the Istanbul region still has plenty of white space. “We see an important distinction between generations,” says Öcal. “While our more established customers tend to prioritize quality, exclusivity and long-term value, Gen Z and younger millennials are more experimental, trend-conscious and open to discovering emerging designers and brands.”

The importance of physical retail in Türkiye is another advantage. Euromonitor’s findings revealed that brick-and-mortar stores dominated personal luxury goods distribution in the nation last year.

Beymen’s Tersane flagship location opened last year.

“The importance high-net-worth consumers place on personalized service and exclusive shopping experiences makes physical stores indispensable for luxury brands,” argues Zeydanlı. “I believe independent designers and local brands are becoming increasingly visible. Consumers are looking beyond global fashion houses and are also interested in discovering brands with a distinctive design identity, more limited production and a unique creative perspective.”

Communité is an experiment in the market. Prospective competitors will be watching closely to see if it lands or if it’s just too soon.

Matt, 45, a firm owner based in Istanbul, is trying on a Beymen Club (the group’s own brand) knit in Beymen’s Galataport location. He opts for brands that aren’t “too vulgar”, preferring what he calls “silent luxury”. “I don’t like clothing with huge brand [logos] on them,” he says. “This is one of the places you can find the stuff that [I’m] looking for.” Annually, his typical clothing spend sits at no more than around $5,000 per year. “I don’t shop very often to be honest with you,” he says. For Matt, the country’s luxury sector isn’t especially different from other countries, although he does note a preference among consumers for more visibly branded clothing.

Originally from Germany, Ayliz, 22, owns her own brand. Her store is around the corner. She’s posing for a photo in Nişantaşı when I stop her to ask what she makes of the Turkish fashion landscape. “I think Türkiye follows world trends. So, people my age, we wear things that are viral now on social media,” she says. As a shopper, she’s drawn to high luxury, citing Loro Piana and Chanel, and she prefers physical retail. “100% in-person. I have to feel the texture, and see how it looks on me.” She sees Türkiye as a place where you can shop “everything you want”, offering far more stores than her home country.

Miray, 43, an executive vice president in marketing and sales, is taking a meeting in Zorlu Center mall. She used to shop here, but nowadays less so, as she currently resides on the Anatolian side of the city. For her, Türkiye is unique for its customer experience. “Beymen provides a very unique experience,” she says. The store is special because of its brand offering and ease, and she has shopped with the retailer for more than 10 years. She does admit, however, that sometimes she buys brands in Europe (London or France), where they can be cheaper. “I love Burberry, but I’m not a fan of only one brand,” she says. “If I see something good, I buy it. Price and quality are important, and experience also — very crucial.”

Burak, 49, a cost controller in the restaurant sector, prefers shopping online. He’s in the Zorlu Center when I bump into him. He likes brands such as Levi’s and Carhartt for apparel, while for footwear, he opts for Nike and Autry. He’s also into Japanese brands, which he noticed on a visit to Communité. What does he think is unique about Türkiye’s fashion landscape? “It’s mostly haute couture, dresses — I don’t see any [local] designers. They [the retailers] buy outsider [brands], but I don’t like them.”

Başak, 48, currently unemployed, is visiting Zorlu Center mall. She lives on the Asian side, so would typically shop in the Emaar Square Mall. She tells me she isn’t committed to any specific brands, although I note her Michael Kors bag. “When I have the time, I like to shop in person,” she says, although she enjoys both online and physical retail. Her approach to shopping? Meet friends, then shop.

Born and raised in Istanbul, 24-year-old graduate Umut tells me his name means “hope” in English. He’s just dropped into Shopi Go in Nişantaşı and is now standing outside. What brands does he like? “For T-shirts, I like Prada, but for sunglasses, I like Off-White — the Virgil [Abloh] versions,” he says. These days, he typically opts for Adidas footwear. “I don’t like the new Nike designs.” As for his thoughts on Nişantaşı: “It’s mostly luxury. You feel like it’s better quality here.”

#6538. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

#6536. 31 Thanksgiving Dinner Alternatives to Turkey

Honestly, anything can make for an alternative Thanksgiving dinner. It’s your house, your rules. Our only suggestion: Make it festive, fun, and at least a little decadent.

A classic Thanksgiving menu is all well and good, but one of our colleagues swears by serving nachos on the fourth Thursday of every November. If a big bloomin’ bird just isn’t ca-caw-caw-calling your name this year, serve a whole roast fish, pork tenderloin with sour-sweet cherry sauce, or a flaky carrot Wellington instead.

Or go completely rogue with lobster pasta or a big pot of chili. You can do that. Below, find vegetarian centerpieces, celebratory roasts, chicken dinners, and seafood mains for a Thanksgiving that looks a little different. BA’s Best Pumpkin Pie can stay.

Can carrots really count as a main course? They can when they’re roasted, glazed, and tucked into puff pastry with goat cheese, Gruyère, and walnuts. This Wellington feeds 8 to 10.

Red wine, browned mushrooms, pearl onions, and carrots give this meatless braise plenty of heft. Ladle it over mashed potatoes for a vegetarian anchor to your Thanksgiving menu.

Ruffled savoy cabbage, melty cheese, and a buttery cream cheese crust make this free-form tart worthy of the holiday table. Cut generous wedges for dinner and stick with savoy: Ordinary green cabbage won’t work here.

A make-ahead casserole, like this pumpkin-infused strata scented with nutmeg and herbs and balanced by sharp cheddar, is just what your holiday schedule needs. Assemble it the night before; bake it on Thanksgiving.

Turkey isn’t the only holiday cooking project worth clearing the counter for. Delicate homemade crepes are rolled around ricotta, mozzarella, and Parmesan, then baked in marinara. Make the batter and filling a day ahead to split up the work.

Kale, pinto beans, and charred poblanos make these cheesy enchiladas a satisfying holiday main for four to six. Get a head start by making the charred salsa verde up to three days ahead.

This autumnal risotto works as a standalone dinner or alongside your favorite Thanksgiving sides. Set the table with shallow bowls and pick a fall salad full of color and crunch to balance the buttery rice.

British beef Wellington meets Cantonese barbecue-style pork in Peter Som’s pastry-wrapped centerpiece. A shiitake mushroom filling and gravy made from the marinade complete the picture; assemble the Wellington a day ahead.

These impossibly tender short ribs are begging to be served with mashed potatoes and buttery milk buns with garlic butter. Give them what they want—and give yourself a head start by braising the ribs the day before Thanksgiving.

Brisket more your speed? Try our Brisket Bourguignon →

Turkey skin has competition. Tender pork belly, crisp crackling, and a hard cider pan sauce make a persuasive case for skipping the bird. Pass the chile vinegar to cut through the richness; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

Ayesha Curry’s spice-crusted prime rib takes its cues from her mother’s braised oxtails, with habanero crema on the side. Prefer a simpler garlic-and-rosemary approach? Try this Low-and-Slow Rib Roast.

For a roast-and-sides Thanksgiving without the turkey, garlic-and-rosemary-rubbed beef tenderloin makes an excellent centerpiece. Rosemary butter dresses the sliced roast, while tangy horseradish yogurt gives everyone something to swipe their next bite through.

Toasted rice, fried onions, and garlic form a dark, peppery crust on this slow-braised pork shoulder. Set out the big platter and pass the coconut-vinegar pan sauce; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

Maybe save the brown sugar-glazed ham for Christmas? This whole leg of lamb makes for a centerpiece that’s just as showstopping. And, like ham and turkey, leftover lamb can be deliciously repurposed in sandwiches.

A platter of sliced pork tenderloin with glossy cherries and browned shallots has plenty of holiday presence without a long roast. Honey and red wine vinegar give the sauce its sweet-sour bite, and frozen cherries are welcome here.

If you’re going to make tamales, it’s a good idea to make a lot of them. Better yet, turn the process into a party, with everyone spreading masa and folding corn husks around the red chile pork filling.

This pasta packs a whole spectrum of holiday flavors into each bite, with crumbles of Italian sausage, shreds of brussels sprouts, and toasted pecans. Streamlining dinner into one dish leaves you more time for Thanksgiving pies.

For some people, spending all Thanksgiving in the kitchen sounds like a good time. For everyone else, there’s this beef-and-bean chili. A can of pumpkin purée thickens the broth, keeping things seasonal without calling for a single roasting pan.

Give homemade fried chicken an even more festive angle with sage and thyme in the dredge and cranberry-mustard sauce for dipping. Start the buttermilk marinade the day before.

This whole roast duck comes with a built-in Thanksgiving side: The duck fat drippings go into basmati rice that cooks while the bird rests. Plan for an overnight dry brine before the glossy pomegranate-honey glaze gets its moment.

Cooking for a smaller crowd? This skillet delivers the stuffing and the bird—chicken thighs, in this case—in one tidy package. Rendered chicken fat enriches the boxed stuffing mix, with dried cranberries and lemon zest brightening things up.

Two diminutive birds make a festive roast for four. A fiery guajillo chile, ginger, and vinegar marinade flavors both the hens and the potatoes beneath them, so the platter arrives with its own very good side.

You just need to make green beans, because this Thanksgiving main is already a two-in-one: Thinly sliced potatoes cook beneath a whole chicken, catching its drippings and crisping around the edges in the same cast-iron skillet.

If your Thanksgiving table could use a little red sauce (and spice), skip the whole bird in favor of this take on chicken parm. Gochujang and gochugaru bring the heat; melted mozzarella keeps things gloriously gooey.

José Andrés turns chicken wings and a colorful assortment of vegetables into a grand centerpiece, with saffron and smoked paprika flavoring the rice. You’ll need a 15" paella pan or comparably sized two-handled cast-iron or cast-aluminum pan.

There’s nothing like pasta to stretch a spendy ingredient (hello, lobster). Serve with a big crunchy salad with Italian dressing and garlic confit toast that diners can pass around for Thanksgiving party vibes.

Presenting a whole fish at the holiday table is wildly celebratory, even when you’re cooking for just two or three. Bring out lettuce wraps, kimchi, rice, and ssamjang so everyone can build each bite a little differently.

A large roasted salmon fillet looks right at home on a holiday platter, especially under a crunchy, garlicky nut salsa. Make the salsa up to four days ahead, then roast the fish when it’s time for dinner.

The stuffing doesn’t have to be a side. Here, crushed boxed stuffing mix joins Parmesan, lemon zest, and parsley in a crisp crust for mustard-coated white fish. Dinner lands on the table in 25 minutes.

This dark, glossy coconut caramel—savory with fish sauce and garlic, sharp with pickled jalapeño brine—turns pan-seared salmon into a holiday-worthy main. Serve with rice to catch every last bit of sauce.

Like many of the best Thanksgiving dishes, this one starts with a good stock. Carla Hall builds a fennel potlikker with celery, onions, and Pernod before layering those flavors into a hearty bowl of shrimp and grits.

#6535. Inside Fashion’s $276 Billion Succession Shakeup

What appears to be a succession story at a handful of prominent luxury companies is, in fact, a defining moment for the wider industry, with the potential to reshape fashion’s competitive map, a new report says.

“Succession is one of the 10 themes that we believe will shape fashion in the next decade,” says the report’s author, Achim Berg, who in 2025 created FashionSights, a research and advisory boutique, after 23 years at McKinsey.

The report “Fashion’s Succession Problem: The Generational Transfer Reshaping the Industry” is an excerpt from a book Berg co-wrote with Paula Trus titled The Future of Fashion. It is set for publication in March by Bocconi University Press. Ahead of its release, Berg shares the report’s key findings with Vogue Business.

Vogue: Why is succession a defining theme of the next decade?

Achim Berg: We built our index while writing the book. It’s called FashionSights Global 100 (FSG100), a database of the world’s 100 largest fashion and apparel companies ranked by revenue. Out of 100 companies, 46 are family-owned. And out of the 46 companies with family dominance, two-thirds (or 30 companies) face a succession challenge, according to our analysis. These 30 companies generated a combined $276 billion in revenues in 2025. The main criteria for companies meeting what we call succession risk is that they are led by the first or second generation, and those who are in charge, which could be advisory, supervisory board or management, are 65 or older. We also added companies that have publicly acknowledged a succession challenge. It’s worth noting that 63% of the companies navigating succession challenges are based in Europe, 30% in North America and the remaining 7% in Asia-Pacific.

Why is this great generational transfer now?

Most of those companies that are around now, with a few exceptions, were founded in the ’60s, ’70s, ’80s, or ’90s of the last century. Ralph Lauren sold his first ties in 1967. In 1975, Amancio Ortega opened his first Zara store. And in 1984, Tadashi Yanai opened the first Uniqlo store. Modern fashion retail is 60 years old.

Either the family has more than 50% share capital, or more than 50% of the voting rights. But also, in some cases, they do not even need to have that much because they are still the biggest shareholders and they call the shots. Some families have special voting rights or legal structures that allow them to play a larger role.

What are some of the ways succession will play out for these companies?

It depends. First, will the departing owner hand over on time? And second, are the heirs as capable as the founders? Succession will occupy a lot of time and energy, and that could derail some of those businesses. Some of that trouble will lead them to M&A in whatever shape and form. Generational handover could accelerate consolidation as families consider partnerships, outside investment or a sale.  We’re only looking at 30 of the largest 100 companies. But you will also find many smaller businesses facing similar succession challenges and looking to sell. It’s not a given that they’re all going to find an acquirer.

When it comes to buyers, established fashion groups could gain scale through acquisitions and expand their portfolios with new brands. We notably see opportunities for stronger Italian luxury groups.

We also see opportunities for new owners from the beauty and eyewear industries. Think about L’Oréal and EssilorLuxottica and the discussion around Armani. They were considered suitable acquirers by Mr Armani himself.  It could also be a good opportunity for those companies to become more relevant in the fashion space.

Last but not least, brand ownership and licensing companies such as ABG, WHP Global and Marquee Brands could offer another route for families seeking an exit. I interviewed [ABG founder and executive chairman] Jamie Salter for my book. He claims publicly that his ecosystem generates $38 billion in annual retail sales by now. So they can do massive acquisitions globally, and they’re looking for global brands to create licensing.

Some successions, however, are expected to proceed smoothly, according to the report.

Yes, the report identifies clear responsibilities, independent oversight and successors tested through meaningful experience as a foundation for successful handovers.  In the white paper, you will see that we consider the handover at Zegna as one of those more positive examples.  Gildo Zegna is the group executive chair. Gianluca Tagliabue is the group CEO. And Gildo Zegna’s two sons, Edoardo and Angelo Zegna, are also now playing a role as co-CEOs of the Zegna brand and are groomed for succession. A succession typically takes 10 to 15 years of preparation, and our observation is that many of the businesses need to seriously engage in those preparations.

#6534. Buttered Nut Squash

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.
